description: We are Team Hyades. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’re building a seamless, interactive interface to make space data fun and engaging.
summary:
HYADES is a first-person 3D game we built in Godot 4. You play the mission director of a small satellite that watches farmland in West Africa for floods. The game follows a real mission from start to finish in four levels. You design the satellite and launch it, then operate it in orbit, bring its data down at a ground station, and finally turn the images into a flood warning for farmers.

Every choice carries forward. If you pick a cheap radio in Level 1, data piles up in Level 3, and in Level 4, flooded fields go unseen. The parts, orbits, and rockets come from real data tables. A tutor explains each choice as you play, and at the end you get a debrief on what you did well and what you could improve in each level.

Most people only ever hear about the launch. They never see the trade-offs behind a mission or why the data matters once it reaches the ground. HYADES lets players learn those trade-offs by making the decisions themselves. It also shows that satellite data is only useful if it reaches the people who need it, in time to act.
details:
What it does and how it works

HYADES is a first-person 3D game where you play the mission director of a small CubeSat that watches farmland in West Africa for floods. You run the whole mission yourself, across four levels:

  1. Launch Segment. You walk around a launch control centre and install parts in every slot: camera, solar panels, battery, radio and pointing system. Then you pick an orbit, a rocket and a mission lifetime, and launch. Every part costs money and adds mass and power draw, and the mission has a fixed budget and mass limit.
  2. Space Segment. You're on board the satellite. You pick farm regions that are passing below, avoid the clouds, and watch your battery and storage while you scan.
  3. Ground Segment. At the ground station you decide whether flood images or crop images come down first, then track the satellite as it passes overhead. Whatever the radio link can't carry stays in space.
  4. User Segment. At an analysis centre you look through the images, mark the flooded plots and choose how to warn people: an emergency alert, a flood map, a crop report or a dashboard.

Every choice carries forward. A cheap radio in Level 1 means data piles up in Level 3, which means some flooded fields in Level 4 have no imagery at all. At the end, a debrief scores each level and lists what you did right and what you could improve, based on what you actually did.

Benefits

Most people only ever see the launch of a space mission. HYADES shows the whole chain behind it: the engineering trade-offs, operating in orbit, getting the data home, and turning it into something useful. Players learn by making the decisions themselves and seeing the results, not by reading about them. A tutor explains each choice in plain language as you go, and the instruments on screen show real quantities like power, storage, contact time and data rates.

Intended impact

We want students and the general public, especially in Africa, to see that satellites are a tool for problems they know, like floods and food security. They aren't just something that happens far away. We hope the game gets players interested in Earth observation and space engineering. It also makes a point we think matters: satellite data only helps if it reaches the right people in time.

Tools and technologies

  • Godot 4 game engine (tested on 4.3 and 4.7), programmed in GDScript. Most scenes, rooms and interfaces are generated in code, which keeps the game light enough to run well on a normal laptop.
  • CSV data tables for missions, parts, orbits, rockets and thresholds. These were built from a shared spreadsheet, with sources noted for each value (for example, the ANDES 6U CubeSat platform for structure mass).
  • 3D models in glTF format, including NASA models of a CubeSat and Landsat 8, an Earth globe, the Moon, and plant models for the farm scenes. A small Python script converted and optimised the models.
  • Git and GitHub for teamwork, plus automated test scenes that play through all four levels and take screenshots to catch bugs.
  • Custom audio management, a game font (Brogame), and saved progress so players can continue later.

What makes it creative

Space mission games usually stop at the launch, and data dashboards are usually dry. HYADES links the two: you build the satellite, then live with your own design decisions for the rest of the mission. Each level has its own room and equipment that look and work like the real thing, from launch consoles to tracking dishes to analysis workstations. The story is set in West Africa, with a short opening cinematic, so the mission has a real place and real people depending on it.

What our team considered

  • Realism vs. fun. The numbers are based on real CubeSat parts and real orbits, but simplified enough that a first-time player can understand them.
  • Balance. We checked every combination of design choices against the data, so that several designs (not all) can launch within budget and mass. That way there's no single right answer.
  • Clarity. One decision at a time at the Mission Console, short descriptions instead of long ones, and a preview of the objectives at the start of every level.
  • Performance. The game runs smoothly on an ordinary laptop, without needing a gaming PC.
  • Scope. We focused on one fully playable mission (Flood Monitoring) and made it complete, rather than four half-finished ones. The other three missions are on the select screen as locked, to be added later.
